messages.content:
You are an evidence extraction specialist for PFAS treatment and remediation
research. Build a structured study evidence table before any narrative review
is written.

Extract one record per primary-study experiment, modeled scenario, or field
deployment that contributes usable evidence to the review task. A paper may
produce more than one record only when materially different matrices,
technologies, operating regimes, or endpoints would otherwise be conflated.

Review articles and perspectives may help identify terminology or primary
studies, but they must not be used as the source of a quantitative study
record. Never copy a review table as though it were a primary result.

For every populated source-dependent field:
- preserve the PFAS identity or class, matrix, starting concentration or
  loading, operating conditions, study scale, measured endpoint, value, unit,
  and material qualifiers when reported;
- attach only the field-level evidence locator identifiers that directly
  support that specific value or statement;
- use an empty string or empty array when the source does not report the
  information; do not infer or estimate it;
- do not turn the absence of information in the supplied packet into a study
  finding, quantitative result, or author-reported limitation unless the source
  explicitly states that absence;
- distinguish removal, separation, sorption, parent-compound loss,
  transformation, degradation, destruction, defluorination, mineralization,
  total organofluorine change, and toxicity change;
- classify endpoint_type from what was actually measured, not from the
  authors' preferred label. Parent loss alone is not destruction. Phase
  transfer is removal or separation, not degradation. Inorganic fluoride
  release or fluorine-balance closure can establish defluorination but cannot
  by itself establish mineralization. Use mineralization only when direct
  carbon-fate evidence such as CO2/inorganic-carbon production or a carbon
  balance is reported. Preserve a broader author term in reported_term and
  explain any mismatch in interpretation;
- do not normalize or compare values unless their units, denominators,
  matrices, PFAS scope, operating conditions, and endpoints permit it.

Only populate quantitative_findings when the source reports an actual numeric
value, inequality, approximate value, range, or explicit ND/not-detected
result. Put the number or censoring marker in value and the measurement unit in
unit. Normalize Unicode inequality signs to ASCII >= or <= and range dashes to
an ASCII hyphen while preserving the source wording in qualifiers. A unit or
order-of-magnitude scale without a number is not a quantitative finding.
Qualitative parent loss, intermediate formation, or disappearance belongs in
the endpoint interpretation or residual/byproduct statements instead.

Set value_form to exactly one of:
- exact_numeric: a bare number such as `99.7` or `1.2e-3`;
- approximate_numeric: `~` followed by a number;
- inequality: `<`, `<=`, `>`, or `>=` followed by a number;
- range: two numbers separated by `-` or `to`; or
- not_detected: exactly `ND`, `N/D`, `not detected`,
  `below detection limit`, or `below quantification limit`.

Put uncertainty, denominators, fold-change wording, and explanatory text in
qualifiers rather than value. A deterministic validator will remove malformed
quantitative fields before source verification.

For limitations, use basis=author_reported only when the source states the
limitation. Use basis=design_inferred only for a constraint that follows
directly from cited design evidence, such as one matrix, one compound, or
bench-scale operation. Never label missing information in the supplied packet
as a scientific limitation of the study.

Mark each record as comparable with conditions, descriptive only, or not
comparable. Comparability is an analyst inference rather than a quotation:
attach locators for the matrix, scale, conditions, endpoint, and denominator
on which the inference rests, and explain the reason. Do not reward a study
for reporting a larger percentage when its endpoint or conditions differ.

The task was derived from a defining review that is held out from all
candidate retrieval systems. The supplied anchor identifiers are an exclusion
list, not evidence. Do not extract from the anchor, cite it, reconstruct its
conclusions, or use its tables.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied evidence-table schema exactly.
Do not write the narrative review in this step.

Task:
{"review_brief":"Prepare a focused review of how water-matrix effects should be tested and reported so that PFAS treatment performance can be translated beyond clean laboratory water.","task_id":"RT10","title":"Designing PFAS treatment studies that remain valid in real water"}

Task-specific data extraction objective:
Extract matrix constituent and concentration, PFAS identity, treatment, clean-water control, matrix-modified condition, direction and magnitude of effect, endpoint, proposed mechanism, constituent interaction, matched operating conditions, and study scale.

Source system (return this exact value):
gpt51_web_search

Candidate source identifier (all records must use this exact source_id):
WEB15

Do not use search-result snippets as evidence. Use only the frozen inspected

resolves to a held-out anchor DOI, URL, or exact title and report the violation

this source, prioritizing records that answer the task components.

Extract primary-study evidence needed to answer the task and return the

extraction_notes: The only accessible information from WEB15 is a high-level description of the experimental framework (batch sorption isotherms, QCM-D, and column tests) and the fact that pH, ionic strength, and natural organic matter were varied to study PFOA and PFOS removal. No specific constituent concentrations, PFAS loadings, or quantitative performance data are present in the supplied extract, so all quantitative fields are left empty and records are classified as descriptive only.
The held-out anchor AR-ZEIDABADI-2023 (doi:10.1016/j.hazadv.2023.100322) was not accessed and was not used as an evidence source for any record.

records.citation: Ultra-high capacity, multifunctional nanoscale sorbents for PFOA and PFOS treatment (preprint, 2023)

comparability.reason: The experiments systematically varied pH, ionic strength, and NOM under matched batch sorption conditions, but the available extract does not report constituent concentrations, PFAS loadings, or quantitative removal values, so matrix effects can be identified qualitatively but not compared numerically across conditions or to other studies.

endpoints.interpretation: Sorption capacity and extent of PFOA and PFOS uptake by nanoscale sorbents were measured in clean laboratory water and in matrices modified with pH, ionic strength, and NOM to quantify matrix effects on equilibrium sorption behavior.
endpoints.reported_term: batch sorption isotherms; PFOA and PFOS removal

endpoints.interpretation: Decrease in aqueous PFOA and PFOS concentration in batch tests was used as a measure of removal efficiency under varying matrix conditions relative to clean water.

limitations.statement: Matrix effects were only probed for two PFAS (PFOA and PFOS) using bench-scale batch systems, which may limit direct extrapolation to broader PFAS classes or full-scale applications.

Specific constituent concentrations (exact pH values, ionic strengths, and NOM levels) and quantitative magnitudes of matrix-induced changes in sorption performance are not reported in the available extract, constraining detailed comparison.

matrix.value: Aqueous laboratory solutions (clean water) with systematically varied pH, ionic strength, and natural organic matter (NOM) to assess PFOA and PFOS sorption and removal

operating_conditions.name: pH
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Batch sorption isotherms conducted across multiple pH values to probe impact on PFOA and PFOS removal relative to clean water controls

operating_conditions.name: Ionic strength
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Electrolyte concentration adjusted to study ionic strength effects on sorbent performance

operating_conditions.name: Natural organic matter (NOM)
operating_conditions.qualifiers: NOM added to otherwise clean water to test competitive sorption or fouling impacts on PFOA and PFOS uptake

residuals_byproducts.statement: Study focused on sorption and removal of PFOA and PFOS; no information on transformation products or degradation byproducts is provided in the available extract.

study_scale.value: Bench-scale batch sorption isotherm experiments with nanoscale sorbents

treatment.value: Ultra-high capacity, multifunctional nanoscale sorbents evaluated via batch sorption isotherms

records.citation: Ultra-high capacity, multifunctional nanoscale sorbents for PFOA and PFOS treatment (preprint, 2023)

comparability.reason: Matrix effects were probed under matched column operating frameworks by varying pH, ionic strength, and NOM, but without reported numeric values or breakthrough metrics, only qualitative insights into matrix influences can be used, not quantitative cross-condition comparisons.

endpoints.interpretation: Column tests monitored PFOA and PFOS removal under varying matrix conditions (pH, ionic strength, NOM), likely via breakthrough profiles or effluent concentrations, to determine how matrix constituents alter dynamic treatment performance versus clean-water operation.
endpoints.reported_term: PFOA and PFOS removal; column tests

limitations.statement: Column experiments investigated matrix effects on PFOA and PFOS removal but, in the available extract, do not provide numerical data on breakthrough behavior, removal efficiency, or the magnitude of performance changes caused by specific water constituents.

The flow conditions, sorbent mass and configuration, and exact matrix compositions are not reported in the extract, limiting the ability to generalize or quantitatively translate the results to other systems.

matrix.value: Flow-through aqueous matrices in column configuration, including clean laboratory water and variants with altered pH, ionic strength, and natural organic matter (NOM) to probe dynamic removal performance

operating_conditions.name: Column operation
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Column tests used to study PFOA and PFOS breakthrough and removal; specific flow rates, empty bed contact times, and bed depths are not given in the extract.

operating_conditions.name: pH
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Column influent pH adjusted to examine matrix effects on dynamic removal relative to clean-water feeds.

operating_conditions.name: Ionic strength
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Influent ionic strength changed (via electrolyte content) to study competition/screening effects on sorbent performance.

operating_conditions.name: Natural organic matter (NOM)
operating_conditions.qualifiers: NOM introduced into influent to assess fouling and competitive sorption under flow conditions compared to NOM-free clean water controls.

residuals_byproducts.statement: The focus of the column tests is separation/removal of PFOA and PFOS via sorption; no information is available in the extract regarding degradation, transformation, or byproduct formation in the column system.

study_scale.value: Bench-scale column tests with nanoscale sorbents operated under flow to assess PFOA and PFOS removal in different water matrices

treatment.value: Ultra-high capacity, multifunctional nanoscale sorbents packed in columns for dynamic breakthrough and removal testing
